newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Greenpeace blocks German oil mill in soya row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Greenpeace blocks German oil mill in soya row.

text.p: Greenpeace activists chained themselves to the entrance gate of a soybean crushing firm on Tuesday to protest against the Hamburg company's decision to use U.S. soybeans which may include genetically-modified material.

Police moved in with bolt cutters to break up the demonstration about three hours after it started. They cut handcuffs and chains which the 35 activists from the environmental group had used to attach themselves to the gate.
An eyewitness said activists were trying to block a shipment of soybean oil and soybean meal to customers.

The company, Oelmuehle Hamburg (Oelag), has been a target of demonstrations by the environmentalist group since last week, when it received the first known shipment of U.S. soybeans from this year's crop in Germany, where opposition to genetically-modified beans is strongest.
Protests by European environmentalists gathered pace this week against the start of sales of the soybeans, which have been genetically changed to withstand treatment with Roundup, a weedkiller.
Greenpeace says the beans, developed by Monsanto Co, are a risky experiment with nature and could harm human health.

"We want Oelag to try and procure beans free of genetic modification and to process only those," Greenpeace campaign co-ordinator Michael Kuehn said. "It's their duty to be upfront about their actions and not to delude the customer."
Oelag said the new beans were safe.

"Greenpeace today blocked the entrance of the plant and demanded declarations we would go without genetically modified beans in 1997/98 now that this year's crop has been mixed in the U.S.," Oelag chairman Arnd von Wissel said.

"They want to block U.S. sowings of genetically modified beans that way. But as a crusher we can only process what our customers require and there is not enough demand for non-modified products, besides we think the new beans are safe."
Von Wissel said crushing schedules would not be changed in response to the protests and a small number of German customers asking to swap soya for rapeseed products would receive those.
He invited a Greenpeace delegation into the plant and explained he did not have enough demand or alternative suppliers to abandon his plans to process U.S. new crop beans.
Greenpeace said an increasing number of domestic food and feeds companies was responding to the campaign and demanding clear labelling.
Von Wissel said, "This whole debate should be carried out by scientists and politicians, not an industrial company."

The new beans make up one or two percent of the total U.S. crop and are mixed in with ordinary soybeans when they come off the farm. U.S. commodity trading giant Cargill said the first exports to Europe had probably arrived at its Amsteram plant 10 days ago and had already been delivered to clients.

A spokesman for the Dutch arm of Cargill cited a cargo of beans delivered from an unspecified North American port on the freighter Amber, which arrived on November 2, to be crushed in the normal way in a process that takes only a few hours.
"The modified beans could well have been in the shipment. The problem is that you just can't tell them apart," he said.
Swiss food giant Nestle SA said it would use genetically altered soybeans in its food products, even though its German subsidiary had said it would not.
Nestle would speed up the introduction of the new ingredients to find out how consumers "really react", chairman Helmut Maucher told the German weekly news magazine Stern.
Cadbury's, the confectionary arm of Cadbury Schweppes Plc said on Tuesday it would use derivatives of genetically-modified soyabeans in its products from next year.
A spokesman said the company believed genetically-altered soyabeans were safe and in any case it was impossible to separate them from ordinary beans.
